pages.brief: Above ground, older worker ants carry food and soldier ants guard the nest; below, younger ants build tunnels and care for the young, while a male ant stands near the queen before dying after mating.

pages.text: The Queen The queen is the leader of the colony, but she doesn’t tell the other ants what to do. The largest of all the ants in the colony, the queen is an egg-laying machine. Some queens can lay thousands of eggs every day. Most colonies have only one queen. When other queen ants hatch, they must fly away and start other colonies. When they start laying eggs, they lose their wings. Queens can also live very long for insects—more than twenty-five years—but when they die, so does the colony. I Can Fly! Like queens, some males can also fly. When they land near a colony, worker ants rip the wings off. Then they rush the male to the queen so the two can mate before the male dies.
pages.brief: The large queen rests in a special chamber laying many eggs, while a winged young queen flies away to start a new colony; near the entrance, worker ants surround a male ant and pull off his wings before rushing him to the queen.

pages.text: Let’s Go Floating Not even water can stop some ants. They climb on top of each other and link their legs until they form a raft or bridge made of their own bodies. Yep, Ants Are Awesome Ants may be small, but they can do awesome things. Thousands or millions of ants working together can build bridges to cross a gap in their path. They can also shape themselves into boats to float across rivers safely. As a group, they can overpower animals hundreds of times their own size for food.
pages.brief: A mass of ants links legs and climbs on top of one another to form a living raft floating across a river; nearby, other ants make a bridge of their bodies across a gap, and a large group swarms over an animal much bigger than themselves.

pages.text: So the next time you come across a trail of ants, stop and watch. Better yet, follow them— just don’t step on their trail. When you see what these little gals are capable of, you’ll understand just how awesome they are.
pages.brief: A child crouches beside a long trail of ants marching across a sidewalk and grass, watching closely and preparing to follow them without stepping on the line; the ants continue steadily toward their colony.

books.title: Jack-o'-Lanterns
books.art_why: The book covers legends and history from before photographs, and the keyword check points to drawing.

pages.text: A festive sight on doorsteps, on porches, and in windows, jack-o’-lanterns are popular Halloween decorations. Jack-o’-Lanterns provides students an introduction to the history of this tradition as well as a glimpse into the creative liberties people have taken over the years to create jack-o’-lantern masterpieces.
pages.brief: Several carved pumpkins with varied faces and designs sit on doorsteps, porches, and in windows as Halloween decorations. The festive jack-o’-lanterns glow in an autumn setting, showing how popular and creative the tradition has become.

pages.text: What Is a Jack-o’-Lantern? Some of them look spooky. Some of them look funny. Some of them look like detailed works of art. Who knew that so much could be done with pumpkins? Carved pumpkins are called jack-o’-lanterns. They are a festive sight in windows and on doorsteps and porches. Jack-o’-lanterns are popular decorations around Halloween. When a light is placed inside the hollow center, a jack-o’-lantern glows in the autumn night.
pages.brief: Carved pumpkins with spooky, funny, and detailed artistic faces sit in windows and on doorsteps and porches. One hollow pumpkin has a light inside its center, glowing brightly in the autumn night as a popular Halloween decoration.

pages.text: Children and adults alike enjoy turning pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. Simple jack-o’- lanterns may have triangle eyes and a toothy grin. Others have scary faces. Some artists carve detailed and festive designs. People started carving pumpkins more than a hundred years ago. Legends say the jack-o’-lantern tradition began even earlier, though, in Ireland. People in Ireland carved their jack-o’-lanterns out of turnips or potatoes.
pages.brief: Children and adults carve pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns with triangle eyes, toothy grins, scary faces, and detailed festive designs. In an earlier Irish scene, people carve turnips and potatoes instead of pumpkins for the same tradition.

pages.text: Why did the Irish start this tradition? And where did the name jack-o’-lantern come from, anyway? Many stories are told about its origins. A common one from the nineteenth century tells of a man named Stingy Jack. The legend says that Stingy Jack was cheap. That’s how he earned his nickname. He also liked to play tricks on everyone. Stingy Jack was so mischievous that when he died, he was cursed to roam the land forever. He had to live alone in the darkness. He carved a turnip and put a light inside to guide him. The Irish called his ghost “Jack of the Lantern” and then simply “Jack-o’-lantern.”
pages.brief: A man named Stingy Jack, known for being cheap and playing tricks, roams alone in darkness after death. He carries a carved turnip with a light inside to guide him, the ghost the Irish called Jack of the Lantern.

pages.text: Modern Jack-o’-Lanterns Eventually, the Stingy Jack tradition became part of a night called All Hallows’ Eve. People throughout Europe lit bonfires. They also wore costumes to keep roaming ghosts away. In Ireland, people hollowed out turnips and potatoes and carved scary faces on them. They placed a light inside to keep mischievous spirits like Stingy Jack away from their homes. These were the first jack-o’-lanterns. Soon, people in Scotland and England started to follow the practice of carving vegetables on this night. The English used beets to make jack-o’-lanterns. All Hallows’ Eve later became known as Halloween.
pages.brief: People in Europe gather around bonfires in costumes to keep roaming ghosts away. In Ireland, Scotland, and England, people hollow turnips, potatoes, and beets, carve scary faces, and place lights inside to keep mischievous spirits from their homes.

pages.text: When Irish, English, and Scottish people immigrated to the United States, they brought the jack-o’-lantern tradition with them. They soon found that pumpkins, which grew in the United States, worked well as jack-o’-lanterns. By the 1920s, pumpkin carving became common across America. Today, carving jack-o’-lanterns is an important part of Halloween, just like trick-or-treating and wearing costumes. Every autumn, people visit pumpkin patches, farms, and vegetable stands to pick just the right pumpkin. About 1.5 billion pounds (more than 680 million kg) of pumpkins are grown in the United States each year.
pages.brief: Irish, English, and Scottish immigrants in the United States choose pumpkins at a pumpkin patch, farm, or vegetable stand. Rows of pumpkins grow in the field as families pick just the right one for carving.

pages.text: Carving Jack-o’-Lanterns Pumpkins that are firm, smooth, and free of marks work well for jack-o’-lanterns. A pumpkin that will stay upright is the safer choice. If it tilts to one side, the light inside may not stay in place. Some people buy carving kits with tools and art patterns to make a great jack-o’-lantern. Other pumpkin carvers use their own tools and designs. Some even carve freehand.
pages.brief: A firm, smooth pumpkin sits upright, free of marks. Carving kits with tools and art patterns lie nearby, while a person carefully uses their own tools or carves freehand, choosing a design for the pumpkin.

pages.text: The first step in carving a pumpkin is to cut a hole in the top. This forms the lid. Always have a parent help out while carving with a knife. Next, the inside flesh and the seeds can be scooped out until the pumpkin is clean and hollow. Many people roast the pumpkin seeds for a healthy snack. People also use the pumpkin flesh to make tasty pies, breads, and soups. No part of the pumpkin need go to waste.
pages.brief: An adult helps a child cut a hole in the top of a pumpkin and lift the lid. They scoop out the inside flesh and seeds, filling a bowl; the seeds and pumpkin flesh can become snacks, pies, breads, and soups.

pages.text: The next step is to draw a design on the pumpkin. When the design is finished, it’s time to carve. People can carve faces, animals, designs, or a message. They can also use stencils or even paint. Every jack-o’- lantern is a special work of art. After the pumpkin is carved, a candle or other light can be placed inside. Then the pumpkin lid can go back on top. It’s best to display a jack-o’-lantern within a few days of carving. After a few days, the pumpkin may spoil and lose shape.
pages.brief: A person draws a design on a pumpkin, then carves a face, animal, or message using stencils or paint. A candle or other light is placed inside the hollow pumpkin, the lid goes back on, and the finished jack-o’-lantern glows.

pages.text: Jack-o’-Lantern Events Many cities host jack-o’-lantern festivals to display their artistic pumpkins. Some of the pumpkins feature traditional scary faces. Creative carvers have also fashioned cartoon characters, animals, and other detailed designs. In Hudson Valley, New York, thousands of jack-o’-lanterns make up a special display. This festive event features sound effects and music. Hundreds of pumpkins lie side by side to form snakes and dinosaurs. The event even has a pumpkin planetarium!
pages.brief: A nighttime jack-o’-lantern festival in Hudson Valley, New York, displays thousands of artistic pumpkins with scary faces, cartoon characters, and animals. Hundreds of pumpkins lie side by side to form snakes and dinosaurs, with music, sound effects, and a pumpkin planetarium.

pages.text: A huge display in Los Angeles, California, features pumpkin cars, dinosaurs, and carvings of sports, television, and movie stars. People can watch as the artists carve their pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns. Giant Jack-o’-Lantern An artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded. It weighed more than 1,800 pounds (816 kg)! The record-breaking pumpkin was as heavy as a cow. The artist beat his own Guinness World Record for largest jack-o’-lantern. He had earned that record five years earlier.
pages.brief: In Los Angeles, California, a huge display features pumpkin cars, dinosaurs, and carvings of sports, television, and movie stars. People watch artists carve pumpkins. Nearby, an artist carves one of the largest jack-o’-lanterns ever recorded, a giant pumpkin as heavy as a cow.

pages.text: Recently, the town of Keene, New Hampshire, broke a world record for the most lit jack-o’- lanterns on display. The town boasted a whopping thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns! Halloween Under the Sea Carved pumpkins are even displayed put carved pumpkins in large ocean tanks each autumn. No one knows what the fish think, but visitors enjoy the festive sight.
pages.brief: The town of Keene, New Hampshire, displays thirty thousand lit jack-o’-lanterns, a world record. In another autumn display, carved pumpkins sit in large ocean tanks with fish swimming nearby, and visitors enjoy the festive sight under the sea.

pages.text: The Tradition Continues Carving pumpkins into jack-o’-lanterns is a fun activity for people of all ages. Pumpkins can be carved with a scary face or detailed artwork, or be used as part of a larger display. However people carve them, jack-o’-lanterns are a sure sign that Halloween is around the corner. Jack-o’-lantern designs are only limited by the carver’s imagination. What kind of jack-o’-lantern would you make?
pages.brief: People of all ages carve pumpkins with scary faces or detailed artwork and arrange them in a larger display. Glowing jack-o’-lanterns signal that Halloween is near, and every design is limited only by the carver’s imagination.

books.title: What Happens When You Flush?
books.art_why: Keyword check says drawing; historical sewage scenes also suit drawn illustrations.

pages.text: When You Flush When You Flush Everyone uses the restroom, but did you ever stop to think what happens to your waste after you flush the toilet? What Happens When You Flush? provides?? students a comprehensive look at where sewage goes and how it is treated in our communities.
pages.brief: A bright bathroom with an open toilet and a hand near the flush handle. Swirling water disappears down the bowl, suggesting the everyday moment after flushing. Simple tiles and a sink keep the scene focused on the toilet and the unseen journey beginning below it.

pages.text: Introduction SWOOSH! You hear this sound every time you flush a toilet. Did you ever stop to wonder where everything that you flush down winds up? Getting rid of waste is often a complex process. That process can stretch over (or under) many miles in your city or town. First, the Flush STEP 3 Next, the broken-down sludge is sent to another machine. Here, all of the solid waste settles to the bottom. The water at the top is sent to a filter that cleans it. Once it’s safe, this water can be sent to a stream, lake, or the sea.
pages.brief: A toilet flushes with a swirling swoosh, sending waste into pipes below the floor. The pipes travel under streets toward a treatment machine where solids settle to the bottom. Cleaner water at the top flows through a filter and out toward a stream, lake, or sea.

pages.text: What Makes Up My Sewage? Where Does Waste Come From? Where Does It Go? Human waste is called sewage. In most homes, it is created by using the toilet, sink, or anything that makes water dirty. If all this sewage reached our drinking water, it would make it unsafe. For more than two billion people worldwide, waste either piles up on the land or runs into lakes and rivers. Millions of people die each year, sick from drinking water that sewage has made unsafe. Sewage treatment experts are working hard to solve this problem, but it is a huge task.
pages.brief: A toilet and sink send dirty water into a sewage pipe. The pipe leads toward a lake or river where people might drink, showing how unsafe water can spread. Nearby, a treatment expert studies the problem, while distant communities face waste piling on land or running into water.

pages.text: Lucky for us, the sewer pipes in our homes don’t just empty into our drinking water. Instead, in many cities and towns, all of this dirty water ends up in the local sewer. Two Underground Systems.
pages.brief: Below a row of homes, small pipes from each house join a larger local sewer pipe. A separate pipe carries clean drinking water, keeping the two underground systems apart. Dirty water travels through the sewer while drinking water stays in its own pipe.

pages.text: Inside the Treatment Plant Small sewer pipes join up to form bigger and bigger pipes. The sewage moves through these pipes to a sewage treatment plant. The water is cleaned there. Things in the water that can make people sick are removed.
pages.brief: Underground, small sewer pipes join into bigger and bigger pipes. The pipes lead to a sewage treatment plant building, where the dirty water is cleaned. Inside the plant, machinery removes things that can make people sick before the water moves on.

pages.text: Not all sewage treatment systems are alike. One common type cleans sewage in the STEP 1 A big screen (think of a giant kitchen strainer) removes large items such as rocks, sticks, and garbage. That way, they don’t jam up the treatment plant’s machines. STEP 2 What is left over after this process is called sludge. It is thick, dirty water. The treatment plant helps bacteria grow in the sludge. These bacteria eat the sludge to break it down.
pages.brief: Inside a treatment plant, a huge screen like a kitchen strainer catches rocks, sticks, and garbage. Below, thick dirty sludge fills a tank. Tiny bacteria grow in the sludge and eat it, breaking down the solid waste so it can be treated further.

pages.text: The Water Treatment Process STEP 4 The solids are sent to a giant tank 1 called a digester. There, a second kind of bacteria eats much of the sludge. 2 The digester breaks down the solid sludge again and pulls more water from it. About half of the sludge turns into gas. Some of the gas helps power the plant’s machines. The other half of the sludge is dried. It’s often used on farm fields to help grow crops.
pages.brief: A giant digester tank holds solid sludge while a second kind of bacteria breaks it down. The tank pulls more water from the sludge, and about half turns into gas. Pipes carry some gas to power plant machines. Dried sludge is spread on farm fields to help crops grow.

pages.text: The Septic Tank The Septic System— Another Way to Deal with Waste Many homes in the country are far from each other. Building a system large enough to serve homes so far away from one another wouldn’t make much sense. Instead, each home sends human waste into a septic tank. This is a small sewage treatment system for only one home.
pages.brief: A single house stands far from neighbors in the countryside. In its yard, a small septic tank is buried underground. Waste from the home flows into this tank instead of a large city sewer, because building long sewer lines to distant homes would not make much sense.

pages.text: The septic tank is buried in the yard near the home. Any waste from the home runs into the tank. Inside the tank, the solids drop to the bottom. The liquid runs out through underground pipes into the yard and spreads into the soil. The liquid is filtered as it moves through the soil. This pulls out harmful things before they reach drinking water. The septic tank collects all of the solid builds up over time. When there is too much sludge in the tank, a septic pump it out.
pages.brief: A cutaway view shows a septic tank buried in a yard beside a home. Solid waste settles at the bottom while liquid flows through underground pipes into the soil. The soil filters the liquid before it reaches drinking water. A pump hose removes built-up sludge from the tank.

pages.text: Sewage Through the Ages Think these systems are yucky? Think again. The first sewerage systems were built thousands of years ago in places such as the Middle East. These early systems sent human waste with harmful bacteria away from cities—and directly into nearby water. The water made people sick.
pages.brief: An ancient Middle Eastern city shows early sewerage channels carrying human waste away from buildings and directly into a nearby river. The channel water reaches people who use the river, suggesting how harmful bacteria in the waste could make them sick.

pages.text: Even by the 1800s, large cities like New York still had a hard time with their waste. People’s homes had no toilets. Sometimes they just had a hole in the ground. Since there was no way to flush, human waste would pile up in the hole. Some people allowed their waste to spill over and wash into the streets. It would pile up where people walked and children played. The smell was awful.
pages.brief: An 1800s New York street scene shows homes without toilets. A hole in the ground holds human waste, and some waste spills into the street. Piles collect where people walk and children play, with wavy lines suggesting an awful smell.

pages.text: Experts began to understand that streets flowing with waste were making people sick. New York City began building sewerage systems so the waste would have somewhere to go. By 1914, it had nearly 850 miles (1,368 km) of sewer lines. Today in the United States, waste disappears down toilets and sinks as if by magic. Now you know how it really works, though. So the next time you flush, take a moment to thank your modern sewerage system!
pages.brief: Workers lay long lines of new sewer pipes beneath a New York City street, part of a system that grew to nearly 850 miles by 1914. In a modern bathroom, a toilet flushes waste away. The scene contrasts early sewer construction with today’s hidden system.

books.title: Route 66
books.art_why: The book spans past decades and historical road scenes best shown in drawn reconstructions.

pages.text: Introduction It’s 1957. You take the top down on your red sports car. Rock ’n’ roll music blasts from the speakers. Ahead of you is nothing but open road. Could this drive get any better? Then you pass an ice cream cone that’s three stories tall. Your mouth waters. Should you stop? Wait—there’s a cheeseburger the size of a bus. Time for a quick lunch instead! When it’s time to rest for the night, you park next to a hotel room shaped like a teepee. What a fun day it was on the road! Who knows what tomorrow will bring? You’ve just taken a road trip down America’s favorite highway, Route 66.
pages.brief: A red sports car with the top down speeds along an open road in 1957, rock ’n’ roll blasting from its speakers. Ahead rise a three-story ice cream cone and a cheeseburger as big as a bus. The driver parks beside a motel room shaped like a teepee.

pages.text: America’s Main Street Have you ever seen a road map of the United States? It looks a lot like a spiderweb. Huge highways zigzag from coast to coast. They connect nearly every city in between. Getting around is easy. Just jump in a car and hit the road! A hundred years ago, driving across the country wasn’t quite so easy. Most “roads” were just small dirt trails. Cars often broke down, got stuck in mud, or popped tires on jagged rocks. In the 1920s, the United States government created new highways to make driving easier. One highway stretched 2,400 miles (3,862 km) from Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California. Its name was Route 66. Some people it the "Main Street of America.”
pages.brief: A road map of the United States looks like a spiderweb, with huge highways zigzagging from coast to coast and connecting cities. Earlier dirt trails leave cars broken down, stuck in mud, or with popped tires on jagged rocks. A new highway, Route 66, stretches 2,400 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles.

pages.text: In 1929, hard times hit the United States. Many banks failed. People lost their money, jobs, and homes. The period that followed was known as the Great Depression. Then a series of long periods without rain destroyed many farms. This time period was known as the Dust Bowl era. Suddenly, many people were forced to leave their homes. Many believed they could find jobs in California. Thousands packed up their belongings and made the long journey west. How did they get there? On a new road named Route 66. The Dust Bowl The Grapes of Wrath, by John Steinbeck, is a classic novel published in 1939. It is about a family fleeing Oklahoma during the Dust Bowl era. They make the long journey down Route 66 to seek work in California.
pages.brief: During the Great Depression after 1929, banks fail and people lose money, jobs, and homes. Long periods without rain destroy farms in the Dust Bowl era. Thousands pack belongings and travel west on Route 66 toward California, hoping for work. A family from Oklahoma makes the same journey in a classic novel.

pages.text: On December 8, 1941, the United States entered World War II. Soldiers from all over the country had to move to military bases in the West. How did they get there? On Route 66, of course! Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels opened up along the route to serve them. When the war ended in 1945, Americans celebrated. Many bought new cars. They drove west to see sights like the Grand Canyon by way of Route 66!
pages.brief: On December 8, 1941, the United States enters World War II. Soldiers travel west on Route 66 to military bases. Restaurants, gas stations, and hotels open along the route to serve them. After the war ends in 1945, Americans buy new cars and drive west to see the Grand Canyon by way of Route 66.

pages.text: Route 66 in Popular Culture The years after World War II were great days for Route 66. Shiny new cars and yellow cabs traveled up and down the route. In 1946, a song called “Route 66” became a top hit. The song told listeners to “get your kicks on Route Sixty-Six.” This song helped make the highway famous. Then, in 1960, a TV show called Route 66 followed two friends who drove across the country. They were looking for adventures on the road. By 1970, most of the original Route 66 was bypassed by a new highway. However, Route 66 remained part of American popular culture.
pages.brief: After World War II, shiny new cars and yellow cabs travel Route 66. In 1946 a hit song tells listeners to get their kicks on the highway. In 1960 a TV show follows two friends seeking adventure on the road. By 1970 a new highway bypasses most of the original route, but Route 66 remains in popular culture.

pages.text: In the year 2000, John Lasseter, the head of Pixar Animation Studios, drove down Route 66 with his family. He fell in love with the colorful art and buildings. He decided to turn his experiences into a Disney-Pixar movie called Cars, which was released in 2006. Lasseter sent a team down Route 66 to do research for the movie. Some of the roadside art they found ended up as characters in Cars. They used Route 66 sights in the movie. For example, the Wigwam Motel in Holbrook, Arizona, became the Cozy Cone Motel. Many families who saw Cars took their own vacations along Route 66. This helped the route become popular again.
pages.brief: John Lasseter, head of Pixar Animation Studios, drives Route 66 with his family in 2000 and loves the colorful art and buildings. He sends a team to research the route for the Disney-Pixar movie Cars, released in 2006. The Wigwam Motel becomes the Cozy Cone Motel, and families take Route 66 vacations.

pages.text: Route 66 Attractions CANADA PACIFIC OCEAN UNITED STATES 1 CA 2 Route 66 IL A MO ATLANTIC OCEAN AZ OK @ NM TX MEXICO 1 7 2 8 3 9 4 @ 5 A 6 Roadside Attractions Museums, motels, and shops are found all along Route 66. Route 66 is also full of unique art, historic gas stations, and theaters. In addition, travelers can see live shows such as a Native American dance or a rodeo. One thing’s for sure—you won’t be bored on Route 66!
pages.brief: Along Route 66, travelers find museums, motels, shops, unique art, historic gas stations, and theaters. They can watch live shows such as a Native American dance or a rodeo. A map of the United States shows Route 66 crossing the country, with many roadside attractions to explore.

pages.text: Cadillac Ranch In 1974, some artists buried ten cars nose down in a field. Visitors have covered them with colorful spray paint.
pages.brief: In 1974, artists bury ten cars nose down in a field at Cadillac Ranch. Visitors cover the cars with colorful spray paint. The cars stand in a row, transformed into a bright, painted roadside attraction.

pages.text: Elmer's Bottle Tree Ranch Folk artist Elmer Long built Bottle Tree Ranch out of recycled bottles, car parts, and other found objects. When wind blows through the open bottles, the air fills with music. Blue Whale What do you give the woman who has everything? Hugh Davis built his wife an 80-foot (24.4 m) blue whale for their anniversary!
pages.brief: Folk artist Elmer Long builds Bottle Tree Ranch from recycled bottles, car parts, and found objects; wind blowing through the open bottles fills the air with music. Hugh Davis gives his wife an 80-foot blue whale for their anniversary, creating another roadside attraction.

pages.text: A Land of Giants Route 66 is truly a land of giants. A California factory sold thousands of huge statues to businesses to use for advertising. The factory added costumes to turn the giants into cowboys, astronauts, and even chickens. Many of the biggest statues on Route 66 are food statues. Huge oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones might make your mouth water. Look out the window in Illinois to see the largest catsup bottle in the world!
pages.brief: A California factory sells thousands of huge statues to businesses for advertising. The factory adds costumes, turning the giants into cowboys, astronauts, and chickens. Many of the biggest statues are food: huge oranges, donuts, cheeseburgers, and ice cream cones. In Illinois, travelers can see the largest catsup bottle in the world.

pages.text: Dinosaurs by the Dozen Route 66 is home to prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. One of these giants might be the largest concrete dinosaur in America. He is 150 feet (45.7 m) long and lives at a dinosaur park in California. Claude Bell built the park to draw visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn.
pages.brief: Route 66 is home to prehistoric creatures of all shapes and sizes. One giant might be the largest concrete dinosaur in America, 150 feet long, living at a dinosaur park in California. Claude Bell built the park to draw visitors to his nearby restaurant, the Wheel Inn.

pages.text: Saving Route 66 As more people visited Route 66, heavy traffic caused damage to the highway. From 1956 through the 1980s, new high-speed highways with many lanes were built around Route 66. As more travelers used these highways, businesses on Route 66 lost customers, and many closed. Peeling paint and boarded-up windows became common sights. In 1999, the United States Congress passed a law to protect Route 66. It gave money to help businesses and towns keep important places open. Now Route 66 is growing popular again. The best way to catch the spirit of Route 66 is to drive it. You’re sure to have an unforgettable American experience of your own!
pages.brief: Heavy traffic damages Route 66. From 1956 through the 1980s, new high-speed, many-lane highways are built around it. Businesses lose customers and close, leaving peeling paint and boarded-up windows. In 1999, Congress passes a law to protect Route 66 and give money to help towns keep important places open. The route grows popular again.

books.title: Sled Dogs to the Rescue
books.art_why: The book uses colorful illustrations for a 1925 historical relay, so drawing fits.

pages.text: Sled Dogs to Sled Dogs to the Rescue tells the true story of the Alaskan sled dog teams and their mushers who raced through wind and snow in 1925 to deliver medicine to the sick. They had to overcome great obstacles to save the day. Colorful illustrations accompany this text about an important event in history.
pages.brief: A team of sled dogs pulls a musher’s sled through wind and deep snow in Alaska in 1925, racing to carry medicine to sick children. The dogs lean into the storm, the musher holds the sled, and the frozen wilderness stretches around them.

pages.text: A Terrible Disease In January 1925, sled dog teams raced in a blizzard from team to team. Many times, the mushers through the wilderness of Alaska. They battled through heavy snow and icy had to stop to warm the medicine by a fire. winds to save children’s lives. Some of the dogs did not survive the journey.
pages.brief: In a blizzard in the Alaskan wilderness, a musher kneels beside a small fire, warming a medicine package while his sled dogs wait in deep snow. Other dog teams battle heavy snow and icy wind; one exhausted dog lies still in the snow.

pages.text: It all started when a terrible disease spread through the town of Nome, Alaska. Two Native children died. Then others became very sick. They needed medicine right away. Nome’s only doctor ordered medicine. However, none came before the city’s port shut down for the winter. The medicine that could save the children was in Anchorage, almost 1,000 miles (1,600 km) away.
pages.brief: In Nome, Alaska, a doctor tends sick Native children in bed while worried families gather nearby. Outside, the winter port is shut and icebound. Far away in Anchorage, the medicine that could save the children waits, almost 1,000 miles from Nome.

pages.text: The medicine could be delivered part of the way by train. Even so, it was 674 miles (1,085 km) from the last train stop to Nome. The distance was too great for airplanes of that time to fly safely. Sled dogs were first used by Native people to deliver goods in the snow. It was clear that sled dogs were the best way to deliver the medicine. There was a problem, however. The distance was too far for one sled dog team. A relay was the only hope.
pages.brief: At a snowy train stop, a medicine package is unloaded near a waiting Native Alaskan musher and sled dog team. A small early airplane sits grounded nearby. The dogs must carry the medicine 674 miles toward Nome, too far for one team alone.

pages.text: The Great Sled Dog Relay More than 20 top mushers, most of them Native Alaskans, were set to take part in the relay. More than 150 sled dogs would also take part. Mushers would hand off the medicine to the next team at different posts along the way. On January 27, the medicine arrived by train where the first sled dog team waited. The package, wrapped in heavy fur to keep the medicine from freezing, was handed off. Alaska The race to Nome was on. The dogs battled through rough wilderness and high winds in GULF OF bitterly cold weather. The medicine was passed ALASKA.
pages.brief: More than twenty Native Alaskan mushers and over 150 sled dogs gather at relay posts in the Alaskan wilderness. At a train stop, a musher receives the medicine wrapped in heavy fur and passes it to the next team. High winds and bitter cold surround them.

pages.text: One of the teams was driven by the famous musher Leonhard Seppala. It covered the most dangerous part of the race. The temperature had fallen to –85 degrees Fahrenheit (–65°C). Seppala’s lead dog was a twelve-year-old Siberian husky named Togo.
pages.brief: Leonhard Seppala drives his sled dog team over a dangerous, wind-scoured trail in bitter cold. At the front runs Togo, his twelve-year-old Siberian husky lead dog. Frost covers the dogs and musher as the temperature falls to minus eighty-five degrees Fahrenheit.

pages.text: To save time, Togo and his teammates raced over an area of frozen sea in the darkness. The next day, they struggled up snow-packed mountains. They traveled an amazing 91 miles (146 km)—more than any other team.
pages.brief: In darkness, Togo and his teammates race across an area of frozen sea to save time. The next day, they struggle up snow-packed mountains. By the end, Togo’s team has traveled ninety-one miles, more than any other team on the relay.

pages.text: The Dogs Deliver The sled dog teams continued their difficult journey. Gunnar Kaasen and his lead Siberian husky, Balto, left on the second to last leg. They raced through a terrible blizzard.
pages.brief: Gunnar Kaasen and his lead Siberian husky, Balto, set out on the second-to-last leg of the relay. They race through a terrible blizzard, with snow swirling around the sled and dogs as the team pushes on toward Nome.

pages.text: Balto led the team through whiteout conditions. At one point, a powerful gust of wind flipped the sled over. The medicine fell in the snow. With bare hands, Kaasen dug through the snow to find the medicine. The bitter cold harmed his fingers, but the medicine was safe.
pages.brief: Balto leads the team through whiteout conditions. A powerful gust flips the sled over, and the medicine falls into the snow. Gunnar Kaasen digs with bare hands through the drift to find it; the bitter cold harms his fingers, but the medicine is safe.

pages.text: When Kaasen arrived at the hand-off point, the next team was not ready to leave. Kaasen decided to continue on to Nome himself. Just before dawn on February 2, Balto and his teammates arrived in Nome. The journey took only five and a half days. The medicine saved the sick children and stopped the spread of the disease.
pages.brief: Just before dawn on February 2, Gunnar Kaasen and Balto bring the exhausted team into Nome. Townspeople and sick children watch as the medicine arrives. After five and a half days, the relay has saved the children and stopped the disease from spreading.

pages.text: After the Race A year after the race, Seppala took his dogs, including Togo, on a tour across the United States. They drew large crowds. He was one of the first to bring the Siberian husky breed to other parts of the country.
pages.brief: A year after the race, Leonhard Seppala takes Togo and his other dogs on a tour across the United States. Large crowds gather to see the famous sled dogs. Seppala helps bring the Siberian husky breed to other parts of the country.

pages.text: That same year, a statue of Balto was built in New York City. Balto and some of his teammates were in a dog show that toured the United States. However, they were not treated well. A businessman from Cleveland, Ohio, was upset. He thought the dogs had earned a better life. He arranged for their story to be published in a newspaper. In just ten days, people gave enough money to bring the dogs to Cleveland. They stayed in the Cleveland Zoo for the rest of their lives. Balto is still famous for his bravery. However, every sled dog on that journey helped save the sick children when little hope was left.
pages.brief: In New York City, a bronze statue of Balto stands as a tribute. Balto and some teammates, once poorly treated in a touring dog show, are brought to the Cleveland Zoo after people donate money. They live there for the rest of their lives, remembered for helping save the children.

books.title: I Collect That!
books.art_why: Real collectors and real collectible objects exist today, so photographs suit the book.

pages.text: Collecting things can be an enjoyable hobby. I Collect That! is an entertaining book that introduces students to the concept of a collection and provides many examples of people’s interesting and sometimes odd arrays of objects.
pages.brief: A tabletop filled with separate, neatly grouped collections of objects—rocks, stickers, toy cars, cards, shells and small souvenirs—each group arranged together to suggest the many kinds of collections the book will introduce to readers.

pages.text: Introduction Do you own a few stuffed animals, video games, or other items that are similar to one another? Then you have a collection and can call yourself a collector!
pages.brief: A child in a cozy room stands beside a shelf holding a few stuffed animals and a stack of video games, all similar items grouped together, showing with a smile that owning alike things makes a collection.

pages.text: A collection is a group of objects that are alike. People collect all sorts of things, such as rocks, stickers, cars, and even dirt from different places!
pages.brief: Four small groups of alike objects are arranged side by side: smooth rocks, colorful stickers, toy cars, and small jars of dirt from different places, each group showing a collection of similar things gathered together.

pages.text: Collecting Is Cool Collecting things is a great hobby. People collect things that excite them and keep their interest. Different people have different interests. Some people are interested in action figures, while others prefer leaves. Collections can be big or small. You might have trading cards or ten comic books.
pages.brief: A group of people of different ages show collections that interest them: a child holds action figures, another arranges leaves, and others display trading cards and a stack of comic books, all looking pleased with their hobbies.

pages.text: Collecting can bring people together. Meeting and talking to people who collect the same things can help you learn more about your collection. You can also buy, sell, and trade parts of your collection. Do You Know? Collectors often get together at meetings called conventions to learn more about what they collect. Huge conventions happen all over the world for collectors of all kinds of things— from dollhouses to toy trains.
pages.brief: At a busy collectors' convention in a large hall, people meet and talk around long tables displaying dollhouses and toy trains, some buying, selling and trading items while others examine collections together with clear interest.

pages.text: Keeping a collection can be hard work. Many collectors keep count of their items and take care of them. Collectors usually sort their objects in some way. They might look at age, size, type, or material.
pages.brief: A collector at a table carefully counts and takes care of a collection, sorting objects into separate groups by age, size, type and material, with neat piles arranged around them, showing the effort of keeping everything organized.

pages.text: Common Collections Stamps, coins, masks, and dolls are some of the most popular collect. These items are easy to find, and there are many different kinds. People can collect coins or stamps from one country or from many the world. Math Minute Emma counts 34 bookmarks in her collection. She gets 11 more for her birthday. How many bookmarks are in her collection now?
pages.brief: A display of popular collections: stamps and coins from one country and from many around the world, masks, dolls, and a girl named Emma counting a large group of bookmarks after getting more for her birthday.

pages.text: Some people collect things from places they have visited. When they travel somewhere new, they buy a souvenir. It might be a magnet, key chain, or snow globe with the name or picture of the place.
pages.brief: A traveler in a busy souvenir shop chooses a magnet, a key chain and a snow globe decorated with the place they have visited, ready to take home as reminders of the trip, while shelves nearby hold more vacation keepsakes.

pages.text: Other people collect things they find in nature, such as sticks or shells. They search for items to collect while hiking in the woods or exploring a beach. Many people use their collections to create new things. Some collectors turn their finds into things they can wear, such as a necklace or bracelet made from collected sea glass. Others make works of art. Bottle caps are used to make anything from maps to magnets. Driftwood can be turned into wind chimes.
pages.brief: On a woodland hike and a beach walk, collectors gather sticks, shells and sea glass. Later, hands turn the finds into a sea-glass necklace, a bracelet, bottle-cap art and wind chimes made from driftwood, showing natural collections becoming new things.

pages.text: You Collect What? Some people collect objects based on a specific theme, such as a type of animal. One woman set the world record for owl collectibles. She owns more than eighteen thousand things related to owls—owl toys, owl T-shirts, and more. Wowser! Barney Smith’s collection of toilet seats became so large that he made a museum to display them. These aren’t regular toilet seats—they’re works of art! Stop by the Toilet Seat Art Museum in Texas to check out his collection of more than one thousand toilet seats.
pages.brief: A woman surrounded by more than eighteen thousand owl-related items, including owl toys and T-shirts, stands near a Texas museum where Barney Smith displays his collection of over one thousand decorated toilet seats as works of art.

pages.text: It takes time to build a collection. It can be rewarding to find an item you’ve been looking for, such as a particular lunch box. Some people enjoy having to work hard to add to their collection. Other people prefer to collect things that are easy to find or make. A woman even made a museum to house her collection of burnt food.
pages.brief: A collector searches through shelves and boxes for a particular lunch box, showing the reward of a long search, while nearby a woman stands in a small museum built to house her collection of burnt food.

pages.text: Start Your Own Collection If you want to start a collection, you don’t have to look far. You can start in your own house with common items, such as bars of soap or hats. Do you have fruit in your fruit bowl? Check out the sticker labels. One woman has over 10,000 fruit sticker labels in her more than 8,500 banana labels! The next time you eat at a restaurant, grab some sugar packets. One man has a collection of more than 14,000 sugar packets. If you start now, you might have an even bigger collection one day.
pages.brief: At home, a child looks at common collectibles such as bars of soap and hats, a woman displays more than ten thousand fruit stickers including many banana stickers, and a man shows his collection of over fourteen thousand sugar packets.

pages.text: Collections can also be really strange. Some people collect air sickness bags and shopping lists other people have left behind in supermarkets. Collecting things is a fun way to spend your time, meet friends, and learn new things. If you don’t already have a collection, maybe it’s time to start one.
pages.brief: A display of unusual collections: air sickness bags and shopping lists left behind in supermarkets, arranged beside more ordinary collections, while a group of friends talk and enjoy their shared hobby of collecting strange and everyday things.

books.title: Acadia National Park
books.art_why: It includes Wabanaki and settlement history that cannot be photographed today.

pages.text: Acadia National Park Maine Maine Each year over two million people go to witness the beauty of Acadia National Park, where the mountains meet the sea. This diverse landscape offers many activities for visitors, including hiking, fishing, climbing, and simply exploring. Acadia National Park provides students with a look at the history of the park and what makes it a popular destination.
pages.brief: A wide view of Acadia National Park in Maine, where rocky mountains meet the sea. Visitors hike along a coastal trail, fish from the shore, climb a rocky slope, and explore the landscape, showing the park’s beauty and the many activities that draw more than two million people each year.

pages.text: First to See the Sun Acadia National Park is one of the first places in the United States to see the Sun rise. Look on a map and you’ll understand why. Maine stretches farther east than any of the other forty-nine states. Acadia has tall peaks that catch the first rays of sunlight.
pages.brief: The sun rises over Acadia’s tall peaks and the ocean, sending first rays of light across the rocky summits. The bright morning shows why this eastern coastal park is one of the first places in the United States to see the Sun rise.

pages.text: Land That Meets the Sea More than two million people visit Acadia National Park each year. The park packs a lot into a small space: beautiful coastline, islands, forests, lakes, and rocks.
pages.brief: A compact coastal park fills the view with rocky shoreline, small islands, thick forests, and quiet lakes. Visitors move along the coast and through the trees, taking in the many different landscapes packed into Acadia’s small space beside the sea.

pages.text: Here, mountains rise from the sea. At 1,530 feet (466 m), Cadillac Mountain is the tallest. Because of its amazing view, it’s also the most crowded. Acadia has more than 40 miles (64 km) of coastline. During low tides, the ocean leaves behind pools of water. Inside these pools live sea stars, sea cucumbers, hot pink seaweed, and more.
pages.brief: Cadillac Mountain rises from the sea, its rocky top crowded with visitors enjoying the wide view. Below, low tide leaves pools along more than forty miles of coastline, where sea stars, sea cucumbers, and bright pink seaweed rest in the shallow water among the rocks.

pages.text: Tide pools come and go—just like tides. Try to visit the tide pools when the tide is going out. You’ll have more time to explore them.
pages.brief: Visitors walk carefully among rocky tide pools as the tide goes out, leaving shallow water behind. The pools shift with the changing tide, and the receding water gives the explorers more time to look at the small creatures and seaweed trapped in the hollows.

pages.text: Wildlife Acadia is one of the best bird-watching spots in the country— 338 kinds of birds have been seen there. Each autumn, thousands of raptors fly over Acadia as they migrate from Canada for the winter.
pages.brief: Bird-watchers stand on a grassy overlook with binoculars, watching the many kinds of birds in Acadia. High above, thousands of migrating raptors sweep over the mountains and coast in autumn, flying south from Canada for the winter.

pages.text: Return of the Falcon Peregrine falcons are one of the fastest animals on Earth. Long ago, they nested on Acadia’s mountains. Their speed didn’t save them from humans, though, whose actions killed many of them. By the 1960s, peregrine falcons were gone from the park. For years, Acadia worked to bring the falcons back. In 1991, the park saw its first falcon chicks in thirty-five years. Since then, chicks have been born in the park every year.
pages.brief: A peregrine falcon dives fast through the air near a mountain cliff, while down on a ledge an adult falcon sits with fluffy chicks. The scene shows the park’s renewed falcon families after years when the birds had disappeared from Acadia.

pages.text: Compared to many national parks, Acadia is not very big. It doesn’t have many big mammals, either. It has lots of small mammals, though, such as foxes and porcupines.
pages.brief: A fox trots among rocks and low plants while a porcupine climbs over a fallen log nearby. These small mammals live in Acadia’s forests and rocky places, showing that the park has many small animals even though it lacks many large mammals.

pages.text: A Park Made Piece by Piece The most amazing fact about Acadia may be that it became a national park at all. Native people called the Wabanaki lived on the land for 12,000 years. Wabanaki means “People of the Dawnland.” The Wabanaki built canoes, fished, hunted, and gathered plants around the area. The Wabanaki Today The Wabanaki are made up of five tribes. They live in Northern Maine and parts of Canada. Those who live near Acadia build canoes and baskets like their ancestors did. They also guide hunting tourists, sell smoked shellfish, or teach people at the yearly Native American Festival and Basket Makers Market.
pages.brief: Wabanaki people build a canoe near the shore, fish in the water, hunt, and gather plants around the land. Nearby, baskets and smoked shellfish show how Wabanaki people today continue canoe making, basket making, guiding, and teaching at their yearly festival and market.

pages.text: In the 1600s, French settlers took land from the Wabanaki. British settlers moved north in the 1700s and fought with the French. The fighting and diseases brought by the Europeans killed many Wabanaki. They forced others to leave. The land became the state of Maine in 1820. Rich people came to the rocky coastline to buy land and build fancy summer homes.
pages.brief: French settlers take land from Wabanaki people on a rocky coast, while British settlers arrive to fight the French. In the distance, fancy summer homes stand above the shoreline, showing how the land later became Maine and drew rich landowners to the coast.

pages.text: The Wabanaki had protected the land for many years. Now, the rich people who owned it wanted to protect it too. A man named George Dorr and others began to donate land to the government. In 1919, that land became a national park. The Story of Dorr George Dorr lived alone in a grand house on Mount Desert Island. In order to protect the area, he slowly bought bits of land, then turned around and donated them. By the time he died in 1944, he had spent all his money, but Dorr had made his dream come true. Acadia had become a national park. In fact, it was still growing like a patchwork quilt, piece by piece. Even today, landowners continue to donate land around Acadia.
pages.brief: George Dorr stands alone by a grand house on Mount Desert Island, looking over protected land and parcels he bought to donate. Around him, the growing park spreads piece by piece like a patchwork quilt, with more landowners adding land even today.

pages.text: Conclusion Acadia National Park is a place where sea and mountain meet. People come to see them meet and, of course, to watch the Sun rise. After greeting the new day, there is plenty more to see and do in Acadia. Visitors can hike, climb, fish, or ride a bicycle.
pages.brief: Visitors hike, climb, fish, and ride bicycles where Acadia’s sea and mountains meet. After watching the Sun rise over the rocky coast, they spread out along trails and shorelines to enjoy the many things to see and do in the park.

pages.text: If you ever get the chance to visit, do!
pages.brief: A visitor pauses on a coastal trail with a happy expression, looking toward Acadia’s mountains and the sea. The open landscape invites anyone who gets the chance to come and explore the park for themselves.

books.title: Rocky Mountain National Park
books.art_why: Rocky Mountain National Park, its wildlife and roads exist today and are widely photographed, so real photos fit every page.

pages.text: Rocky Mountain National Park Wyoming Rocky Mountain National Park is a place of abundant Colorado wildlife and majestic mountains. It’s also a popular destination for over 4 million visitors every year! Each New season brings a new kind of beauty to the park that is Mexico appreciated by nature lovers, whether they are traveling by car or on foot. Rocky Mountain National Park provides students with a detailed look at the many features of the park and what makes it such a special place.
pages.brief: A wide view of Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado: tall rocky peaks rise behind a still mountain lake, pine forest lines the shore, and a moose stands in shallow water. A road curves through the valley with a few cars driving past, and a wildflower meadow edges the water.

pages.text: The Best of the Rockies Rocky Mountain National Park (RMNP), in Colorado, shows off the best of the Rocky Mountains. The park includes 415 square miles (668 sq km) of natural beauty. The air is fresh and clean. Its mountain lakes mirror high peaks above them. The park is home to mountain lions, moose, marmots, and many other wild animals. Nature lovers can enjoy the park, whether by car or on foot.
pages.brief: A mountain lake mirrors the high, snow-streaked peaks above it, ringed by pine trees. On a grassy slope nearby a moose stands among willows, a marmot sits on a rock, and a mountain lion moves along the distant tree line in clear, fresh air.

pages.text: Young Mountains Rocky Mountain National Park is a small part of the Rocky Mountain Range. The Rockies, as they are called, stretch 3,000 miles (4,828 km) from Canada to New Mexico. Compared to other mountain ranges, the Rockies are young. They were pushed up between one hundred million and sixty-five million years ago. Later on, glaciers moved downhill and carved out their valleys.
pages.brief: An aerial view of the Rocky Mountain Range stretching ridge after ridge to the horizon, from Canada toward New Mexico. Below, a glacier creeps slowly downhill between peaks, and a deep valley carved by ice opens out beneath it, with bare rock and scattered snow.

pages.text: The Rocky Mountains form much of the Continental Divide. This is a rocky spine that runs along North America and divides the way water flows. Water on the western side of the divide flows west toward the Pacific Ocean. Water on the eastern side flows toward the Atlantic Ocean. NORTH AMERICA The Continental Divide United States E D V I I D L T A N E N I T N O C Mexico.
pages.brief: A high rocky ridge runs along the crest of the continent, splitting the land into two sides. On the western slope a stream runs down toward distant lowlands; on the eastern slope another stream runs the opposite way. Snow and bare stone cover the ridge top.

pages.text: From Moose to Marmots Rocky Mountain National Park has several different environments. It has wet areas and forests of pine and aspen trees. Mountain wildflowers dot grassy meadows with bright colors in summer. The trees stop growing at about 11,500 feet (3,505 m). This is called the tree line. Above this line, it’s too cold and rocky for trees to grow. Different RMNP are home to different animals. Elk and deer feed along forest edges. Moose wade in and chomp plants there. Bobcats and a few mountain lions and black bears live in the park, too.
pages.brief: A meadow bright with summer wildflowers sits beside pine and aspen forest. Elk and deer graze along the forest edge while a moose wades in a wet marshy patch, pulling up plants. Higher up the slope, bare rocky ground begins above the last stunted trees.

pages.text: Some animals live above the tree line. They include bighorn sheep, Colorado’s state animal. Marmots are one of the largest members of the squirrel family. They can be spotted on warm, sunny rocks, and they squeak loudly if danger is near. In rocky places, pika dash around. They look like big hamsters but are related to rabbits.
pages.brief: Above the tree line, on a bare rocky slope, a bighorn sheep with heavy curved horns stands on a boulder. A marmot stretches out on a warm sunlit rock nearby, and a small pika dashes between stones. Grey rock and low plants stretch away under a bright sky.

pages.text: About 280 kinds of birds have been seen in RMNP. Eagles and ravens ride on mountain winds. Ptarmigan (TAR-mi-gin) are great at hiding in the open. In summer, their brown and gray feathers blend in with the earth. In winter, their feathers turn white and blend in with the snow.
pages.brief: An eagle and a raven soar on the wind above a mountain ridge. Below, on open ground, a ptarmigan in mottled brown and grey feathers crouches, almost blending into the earth and stones. Beside it a second ptarmigan in white winter feathers stands by a patch of snow.

pages.text: Plan a Visit A visit to Rocky Mountain National Park can be carefree or full of adventure. Inside the park, the roads allow drivers to enjoy great views. Trail Ridge Road is the highest paved road in any U.S. national park. As it climbs up and over the Continental Divide, it reaches more than 12,000 feet (3,658 m). This road is closed in winter, when snowdrifts can be more than 20 feet (6 m) deep.
pages.brief: A paved road climbs and curves over a high mountain pass across the Continental Divide, cars driving along it with wide views of peaks and valleys beyond. In another view the same road lies buried under deep winter snowdrifts, closed, banks of snow taller than a person beside it.

pages.text: For people who want to leave behind the sound of traffic, RMNP has hundreds of miles of hiking trails. Some hikers pitch tents near mountain lakes and rushing creeks. Others follow rocky paths to reach mountaintops. At 14,259 feet (4,346 m), Longs Peak is the park’s tallest mountain. Hikers must be very fit to climb it.
pages.brief: Hikers on a rocky trail wind upward toward a mountaintop. Below, tents are pitched on the shore of a mountain lake beside a rushing creek, with hikers resting nearby. In the distance the sharp summit of Longs Peak rises above the surrounding ridges under a clear sky.

pages.text: Autumn is a special time to visit the park. Aspen leaves turn bright yellow. People also come to watch and listen to elk. In September and October, bull elk use high-pitched calls to attract females, known as cows.
pages.brief: Autumn in the park: groves of aspen trees with leaves turned bright yellow stand against dark pine forest. In an open meadow a bull elk raises his head with his mouth open, calling, while several female elk graze nearby. Golden leaves lie scattered on the grass.

pages.text: History of Rocky Mountain National Park Ute, Arapaho, and other Native peoples once lived in and traveled through the land that is now Rocky Mountain National Park. Some spent summers camped in the beautiful valleys. Settlers and gold seekers began arriving in this part of the Rockies in the mid-1800s. For settlers headed west, these same mountains were hard to cross.They had to drive their wagons over the steep passes. Others built mining towns, including Estes Park, near what later became one of the park entrances. In 1915, the president signed a law creating Rocky Mountain National Park. This was followed by a building boom of lodges and roads nearby. However, much of RMNP is still surrounded by forests and wilderness areas.
pages.brief: A mountain valley where Native peoples camped in summer, with tipis among the trees. Further on, settlers' covered wagons climb a steep pass, and a small mining town of wooden buildings sits below the peaks, shown as it was in the 1800s.

pages.text: A Popular Park Rocky Mountain National Park is one of the most popular national parks in the United States. Each year, more than four million people visit from around the world. During the summer months, the park can get crowded. Sometimes there are traffic jams. Many people now ride buses inside the park rather than drive their cars. Four Million and Counting.
pages.brief: A summer scene at a popular park viewpoint: crowds of visitors from around the world stand beside their cars, and a long line of cars waits in a traffic jam along the road. A park bus pulls up to a stop while passengers climb on.

pages.text: Still, anyone willing to lace up their hiking boots can go on an adventure in this park. It is a national—and a natural—treasure.
pages.brief: A hiker crouches on a rock to lace up hiking boots at the start of a trail, a backpack beside them. Beyond, forest, a mountain lake and rocky peaks open out, with the trail winding away into the park under late light.

pages.text: Manatees have rounded bodies and small heads. They have a paddle-shaped tail that helps them move through the water. Large front flippers help them to steer. pages.text: Habitat and Habits Manatees live in both fresh water and salt water. They like shallow water in bays and rivers and along ocean coasts. They like water temperatures higher than 20 degrees C (68 degrees F). A thick layer of blubber protects them from the cold. But they cannot survive if it gets too cold. Manatees are gentle, harmless creatures that have no way to defend themselves. Staying close to shore keeps them safe from sharks and other predators in the open ocean.

In Australia, they sometimes die when they get caught in nets placed along beaches to protect swimmers from sharks.
